summary: Defines the User-based Security Model for SNMPv3, which provides message-level security. It specifies the procedures for authenticating and protecting SNMP messages on a per-user basis, and includes a MIB for remotely managing the model's configuration. It replaces RFC 2574.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3414 defines the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3. It allows management messages to be authenticated, checked to prevent replay, and optionally encrypted, using secret keys tied to named users.

questions: what is the snmpv3 user based security model
how does snmpv3 prevent replay attacks
what is the snmpv3 time window
how does snmpv3 key localization work
subtitle: How SNMPv3 proves who sent a management message, spots tampering and replays, and can hide the contents.

tldr.problem: Network devices accept management commands over SNMP, so an attacker who can alter, forge or replay those messages could change a device's configuration or falsify what it reports.
tldr.mechanism: The User-based Security Model ties secret keys to named users. Each message carries a keyed digest for integrity and authentication, a time indicator from the authoritative engine to reject stale messages, and optionally encrypted contents.
tldr.outcome: SNMPv3 messages can be authenticated, checked for freshness and encrypted per user. The RFC is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2574 and has since been updated by RFC 5590.

today: RFC 3414 is an Internet Standard (STD 62). It obsoletes RFC 2574 and has been updated by RFC 5590.

sections.title: Threats and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 3414 defines the User-based Security Model (USM), the security model used by SNMP version 3. It works at the level of a single message. The main idea is to use the traditional concept of a user, identified by a userName, and to attach security information to that user.

The principal threats are modification of information (altering a message in transit to cause an unauthorized operation) and masquerade (pretending to be a user with the right authorizations). Two secondary threats get limited protection: disclosure (eavesdropping) and message stream modification (malicious reordering, delay or replay). Denial of service and traffic analysis are explicitly out of scope.

The goals follow from this: verify that a message was not modified, verify the identity of the user it claims to come from, detect messages that are not recent, and, when needed, keep the contents from being disclosed.
sections.plainLanguage: USM protects SNMP messages against tampering, impersonation, and replay. It can also encrypt message contents to prevent eavesdropping. Denial of service and traffic analysis are not addressed.

sections.title: Modules and Users
sections.content:
USM is split into three modules. The authentication module provides data integrity and data origin authentication. The timeliness module protects against delay or replay beyond what normal operation causes. The privacy module protects the message payload from disclosure.

Each user has a userName, a securityName, an authProtocol and authKey, and a privProtocol and privKey. Keys are not accessible via SNMP. The RFC states that there is no confidentiality without both integrity and origin authentication, and neither integrity nor origin authentication is possible without the other. Authentication identifies the user on whose behalf a message was sent, not the specific originating device.
sections.plainLanguage: USM uses three separate functions: one checks that messages are authentic and unmodified, one ensures they are recent, and one hides their contents. Each user has their own secret keys for authentication and encryption, which cannot be read over SNMP.

sections.title: Security Parameters
sections.content:
An SNMPv3 message carries a msgSecurityParameters field, which for USM is an OCTET STRING holding the BER encoding of a sequence of six fields: msgAuthoritativeEngineID, msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots, msgAuthoritativeEngineTime, msgUserName, msgAuthenticationParameters and msgPrivacyParameters.

The boots and time values are integers from 0 to 2147483647. The user name is 0 to 32 octets. A zero-length user name matches no user but can be used for engine ID discovery. The last two fields are defined by whichever authentication and privacy protocols the user has configured.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message includes security parameters that identify which management engine is authoritative, the current time according to that engine, the user name, and fields used to verify authenticity and to carry encryption information.

sections.title: Timeliness and Replay Protection
sections.content:
In every exchange one SNMP engine is the authoritative engine. The authoritative engine's identity and clock are included in the message, so a message meant for one engine cannot be replayed to another and a stale message can be spotted.

Each engine keeps snmpEngineID, snmpEngineBoots (reboots since the ID was configured), and snmpEngineTime (seconds since boots was last incremented). Boots is held in non-volatile storage. The same Time Window of 150 seconds applies to all users.

A non-authoritative engine keeps its own copy of the authoritative engine's boots and time and updates them from authentic messages. The timeliness check is only done when the message is authenticated, so the time values can be trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries the time and identity of the authoritative engine. If the message is too old (outside the 150-second window), it is rejected as a potential replay. Non-authoritative engines learn the correct time from authentic messages.

sections.title: Passwords and Key Localization
sections.content:
A single password is turned into a key Ku using the algorithm described in the appendix. To get the localized key for one authoritative engine, the engine's snmpEngineID is placed between two copies of Ku, and the result is run through the hash function of the user's authentication protocol.

This ensures that a compromise of one device's key does not reveal the keys used with other devices. The password or non-localized key MUST NOT be stored on a managed device; only the localized key SHALL be stored, if at all. If the appendix algorithm is used, passwords must be at least 8 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of storing the same password on every device, USM derives a unique key for each device by combining the password with the device's identifier. This limits the damage if one device's key is compromised.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving, and Discovery
sections.content:
To send, the engine looks up the user, encrypts the scoped PDU if needed, fills in the engine ID, boots, time and user name, and computes the authentication parameters over the whole message.

To receive, the engine parses security parameters, finds the user, checks the requested security level is supported, verifies authentication, checks timeliness, and decrypts if needed. Each failure increments a specific counter and returns an error.

Discovery allows a manager to learn an engine's ID and current time. It sends an unauthenticated request with a zero-length user name and engine ID, receives a Report with the engine ID, then sends an authenticated request with boots and time set to zero to obtain the current boots and time.
sections.plainLanguage:
When sending, the message is built with security information and a digest covering the entire message. When receiving, the digest is verified and the time is checked before decryption or processing.

Before secure communication can begin, the manager discovers the device's engine identifier and its current time by exchanging simple messages.

sections.title: Authentication and Privacy Protocols
sections.content:
Two authentication protocols are defined. HMAC-MD5-96 computes a 128-bit MD5 digest in HMAC mode and carries the first 96 bits; the key is 16 octets. HMAC-SHA-96 does the same with SHA and carries 96 bits with a 20-octet key. HMAC-MD5-96 is the one that MUST be supported; HMAC-SHA-96 SHOULD be.

The privacy protocol is CBC-DES. The first 8 octets of the 16-octet privacy key form the DES key (with the least significant bit of each octet ignored) and the last 8 octets form a pre-IV. A per-packet salt, combined with the pre-IV, forms the initialization vector. Data is padded to a multiple of 8 octets and encrypted in Cipher Block Chaining mode.

Privacy is optional to implement; at least one authentication protocol is required for a Secure SNMP implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication uses a keyed hash (HMAC) to prove the message came from the claimed user and was not altered. Encryption uses DES in CBC mode to hide the message contents. Both use keys derived from the user's password.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that responses with no matching outstanding request be discarded, and that msgID values be chosen carefully across the time window. Time synchronization should use authenticated messages. A command generator sending state-altering messages should wait for an acknowledgement or for the previous message to expire.

Secrets should be changed more often with increased use. To be called a Secure SNMP implementation, an implementation MUST implement an authentication protocol, restrict access to user secrets, implement key localization, and implement the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB.

Sending Report PDUs unsecured can expose a non-authoritative engine to some attacks. Access to the usmUserTable in the MIB should be controlled, for example with the View-based Access Control Model in RFC 3415.
sections.plainLanguage:
Implementations should discard unsolicited responses, manage message identifiers properly, and synchronize time using authenticated messages. User secrets must be protected and changed regularly.

Unsecured reports and unrestricted access to user tables can create security risks, so additional access controls are recommended.

data.title: UsmSecurityParameters
data.code:
UsmSecurityParameters ::=
    SEQUENCE {
        msgAuthoritativeEngineID     OCTET STRING,
        msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots  INTEGER (0..2147483647),
        msgAuthoritativeEngineTime   INTEGER (0..2147483647),
        msgUserName                  OCTET STRING (SIZE(0..32)),
        msgAuthenticationParameters  OCTET STRING,
        msgPrivacyParameters         OCTET STRING
    }
